podcast.title: Isolated Rock Resurgence Post-Trump (2017)
podcast.body: Greta Van Fleet is mentioned as an "isolated example" of a rock band that emerged around 2017, at a time when a widespread explosion in loud, angry rock following the election of Donald Trump did not materialize as predicted based on historical patterns. "There were however some isolated examples, like Greta van Fleet. This is from 2017."

podcast.title: Frankenmuth Hometown and Musical Upbringing
podcast.body: The Kiszka brothers grew up in Frankenmuth, central Michigan, a town of approximately 5,000 residents whose main attraction is the "world's largest Christmas store." Their parents exposed them to classic rock and blues music, including artists like Led Zeppelin, Jimi Hendrix, Joni Mitchell, and 30s/40s folk and blues legends like Muddy Waters and Robert Johnson. "They're really from the middle of nowhere, a central Michigan town called Frankenmuth. In about 5,000, the biggest attraction is the self-proclaimed world's largest Christmas store. This is where the Kiska family grew up."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Inspired by Classic Rock
podcast.body: Greta Van Fleet was mentioned as a "new young band" clearly inspired by "old school classic rock." Their inspiration came from raiding their parents' classic rock record collections, showcasing a trend of contemporary artists drawing heavily from earlier rock styles. "We talked about Great Event Fleet on a previous episode." "They rated their parents classic rock record collection for their inspiration."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 4: The Revivals

podcast.title: Later Exposure to Rock and Roll
podcast.body: While traditional music was prevalent in their early lives, the brothers recall getting into what is commonly known as rock and roll, specifically the 60s British Invasion, around high school. "it wasn't until like, I think about high school that we all started getting into what is, you know, commonly known for his rock and roll, you know, a lot of the British invasion and that sort of stuff."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Nurturing Musical Environment
podcast.body: The Kiszka brothers were raised in a "musically nurturing environment" that extended beyond just music to include film and literature. They were surrounded by traditional music, including early American blues artists like Elmore James, Willie Dixon, Robert Johnson, Muddy Waters, and Howlin' Wolf, as well as folk artists like Arlo Guthrie, Bob Dylan, Joni Mitchell, and John Denver, primarily from their parents' vinyl collection. "we were kind of raised in a musically nurturing environment where it wasn't necessarily just music, but there was a lot of film and a lot of literature. And we had a lot of traditional music, you know, lying around."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Perception as New vs. Old
podcast.body: When Greta Van Fleet emerged in 2017, younger audiences perceived them as "new and fresh." However, older generations, particularly boomers and Gen Xers, immediately drew comparisons to Led Zeppelin's sound from 1971, illustrating a generational divide in musical perception and the phenomenon of musical styles being independently rediscovered. "The kids thought they were new and fresh. But God, didn't Led Zeppelin sound like this in 1971?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Shared Experiences and Artistic Communication
podcast.body: The fact that the three brothers, including twins, shared the same life experiences and picked up on musical influences at the same time contributed significantly to their sound. Their strong familial bond allows for easy communication, especially artistically, enabling them to instinctively understand each other's creative direction, even during live performances. "Yeah, same life experiences that we've shared, commonalities and things like that. And it's very easy to communicate, you know, especially, you know, just in general, but artistically, I think that we're on a, you know, we're on the same page a lot of the time where it's like, well, what creatively has to happen here when we come to a junk share where we're deciding, well, should, you know, what should the guitar be doing here? And I think we're all like, yeah, it should be doing this."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Vocal Style Development
podcast.body: Formed in 2012, Josh Kiszka, the singer, initially lacked his own vocal amplifiers. This forced him to develop a powerful vocal style to be heard over the guitars and drums, which, according to Jake Kiszka, naturally evolved into his Robert Plant-like delivery, likely also influenced by their exposure to old Led Zeppelin records. "Josh, for example, didn't have his own vocal amps, so he had to develop a style where he could be heard over the guitars and drums. And according to Jake, which is what he told me, this is how John ended up with that Robert Plant-like delivery."

xref.title: Baltimore Band in Alternative Hard Rock Scene
xref.body: Turnstile, a band from Baltimore, was mentioned in the context of new young bands inspired by old school classic rock, contributing to the Alternative Hard Rock scene in the 2010s. They were highlighted alongside Greta Van Fleet and The Struts as examples of this trend. "We should also bring in Baltimore's turn style."

xref.title: Comparison to Greta Van Fleet
xref.body: In 2017, when Greta Van Fleet emerged, many older listeners (boomers and Gen Xers) immediately noted a strong resemblance to Led Zeppelin's sound from 1971, highlighting a sense of musical déjà vu despite younger listeners perceiving Greta Van Fleet as new and fresh. "But God, didn't Led Zeppelin sound like this in 1971?"
